items.title: 24-Hour Economy secures $5.5bn project commitments – Advisor
items.description: The 24-Hour Economy programme has mobilised about $5.5 billion in project commitments, largely from the private sector rather than government capital funding, a year after its launch. The 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme was launched in July 2025 and aims to shift the country from an import-dependent, raw material-exporting economy towards a self-reliant, round-the-clock productive economy. Speaking at an engagement with the media in Accra last Wednesday, the Presidential Advisor on the 24-Hour Economy, Augustus Goosie Tanoh, said the programme would rely on the private sector to implement the projects while the government would facilitate the environment for the investments to thrive. Despite its young age, he said the programme had attracted significant investment interest because of the credibility of its economic framework. “It is a young programme, but because of the credibility of the economics around it, we are able to mobilise commitments of $5.5 billion,” he said. Mr Tanoh explained that the programme’s responsibility was to develop viable projects and demonstrate their bankability to attract private capital. “We have to show that Project ‘A’ and Project ‘B’ are bankable. Then you put your money in it,” he said. The presidential advisor added that the government support was mainly limited to administrative and project-preparation costs, including hiring consultants and providing basic equipment such as computers and vehicles. “The only support government gives us is our administrative costs. It takes government support to hire consultants, buy a computer, and buy a vehicle,” he said. Major projects underway Mr Tanoh disclosed that WAPCo’s solar project alone was valued at $1.45 billion, while renewable energy and renewable natural gas projects accounted for an additional $2 billion to $3 billion. He pointed out that project developers must demonstrate sufficient equity before agreements would be signed, particularly for large-scale projects. “If you are doing a project like WAPCo Solar, which is $1.45 billion, you want to make sure the person doing it has more than $1.45 billion as equity,” he noted. The Buipe solar and battery project, which is part of the programme’s pipeline, is expected to generate 1,500 megawatts (MW) of electricity and create 13,000 jobs. The 24-hour programme also targets the creation of 1.7 million jobs by the end of 2028. Mr Tanoh explained that despite public expectations, the 24-Hour Economy is being conceived as a “systematic reconstruction” of Ghana’s productive system, with interventions spanning agriculture, manufacturing, logistics, infrastructure, and access to finance. “We all want the economy to move to a level of capacity utilisation that allows factories to operate at 90 per cent, 100 percent, and to invest in new production lines,” he said. “But you can’t leap from 10 percent capacity utilisation to 100 percent capacity utilisation in one year.” 24-Hour markets clarified Mr Tanoh also clarified that the 24-Hour Economy Secretariat had no jurisdiction or oversight responsibility over the 24-hour markets being developed across the country. He said the markets were being financed by district assemblies and implemented by the Ministry of Local Government and the district assemblies. “Although they use a 24-hour logo, we have no control over the markets. We are not part of deciding where it goes and so on and so forth,” Mr Tanoh stated. He disclosed that the secretariat had been sued four or five times over market projects despite having no responsibility for them.

items.title: Divorce, smartphones and control – BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
items.description: Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy’s broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque – then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds. A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings. She will not take no for an answer. In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses. “If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn’t be here… I have taken my decision,” she says. After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are “mindless” and “deficient in intellect”, to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him. The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban’s rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021. In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres. In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers. The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia – Islamic religious law – they imposed in the 1990s. The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule. Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage. “Ask yourself: ‘Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'” says Sarhadi. “You’ll have to compromise a lot or you’ll lose your dignity and honour.” “Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined,” she responds. Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak. Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman’s husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay. The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her – “otherwise he’d be jailed”. Unsatisfied, Tuba’s father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban’s court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband’s consent. Sarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban’s first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group. He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released. When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor – first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz. Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. “Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast.” If he says any more about the ban, “it will cause trouble”, he adds. But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban’s position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation. He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: “I destroyed it with my own hands. “Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God’s law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God’s will.” In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration. Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car. He says he was previously “responsible for the operations of suicide attackers” in Kabul. “I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys,” he says. “There were areas that needed a long time to plan.” Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians. Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will “make people upset” and could “reopen wounds”. Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases. Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question. He is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government. Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn. “Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter,” says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. “But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn’t offend you.” An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee’s microphone is swiftly removed. Afterwards, he tells the BBC: “I requested for the girls’ schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam.” He adds: “There were other things I wanted to say but they didn’t let me talk more.” Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences. Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting. Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban’s intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat. The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government’s spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid. He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi – revealing it publicly for the first time. In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country. Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study “within our frameworks” and they would “be very active” in society. Why did they fail to keep their word? “We are committed to women’s rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia,” he replies. “We should see everything through the Sharia lens.” Allowing women to work in offices such as his own “would lead to immoralities” and “their dignity would be undermined”, he adds. He says the issue of education for women is “under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it”. When questioned about the Taliban’s crackdown on media freedom, he says: “In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can’t let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can’t broadcast against Islamic laws and rites.” The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban’s heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital. We ask to meet the Taliban’s supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview – we are told it will not be possible at the moment. Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women’s voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city. Two hours’ drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group’s most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents’ old secret cave network. Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s. His superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban. The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics. “Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us,” says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. “We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime.” Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns. Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country’s main problem. “I’m speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power,” says Hoda – not her real name – a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power. “Women can’t accept this situation,” she tells the BBC. “They might advance restrictions but it won’t stay like this forever.” “I think the Taliban are scared of educated women,” she adds. “That’s why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can’t raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban.”

items.title: Gourma : 525 jeunes achèvent la première édition du Camp Vacances Faso Mêbo
items.description: BURKINA-GOURMA-FASO-MEBO-CAMP-VACANCES Gourma : 525 jeunes achèvent la première édition du Camp Vacances Faso Mêbo Fada N’Gourma, 22 août 2026 (AIB)- La première édition du Camp Vacances Faso Mêbo, qui a réuni 525 jeunes issus des régions du Goulmou, de la Sirba et de la Tapoa, a officiellement pris fin ce samedi 22 août 2026 à Fada N’Gourma, avec le baptême de la promotion « Toyiro », une appellation en langue bwaba signifiant « L’avenir nous appartient ». La cérémonie de sortie 525 jeunes du Camp Vacances Faso Mêbo s’est déroulée en présence du Gouverneur de la région du Goulmou, Ram Joseph Kafando, des autorités administratives, judiciaires, militaires, paramilitaires, religieuses et coutumières, ainsi que des parents et des encadreurs des campeurs. Représentant le directeur général de Faso Mêbo, le commandant de la Brigade routière Faso Mêbo de la région du Goulmou, le lieutenant Inoussa Koutou, a indiqué que l’initiative visait à offrir à la jeunesse «un cadre de formation, de discipline, de partage et d’éducation citoyenne ». « Aujourd’hui, vous repartez avec de nouvelles connaissances, une expérience commune et, nous l’espérons, davantage de discipline, de confiance et de responsabilité », a-t-il déclaré. Le lieutenant Koutou a salué la vision du Président du Faso, estimant que « l’avenir du Burkina Faso se prépare aujourd’hui avec sa jeunesse». « Votre première force est votre capacité d’apprendre, réfléchir, travailler et créer. Vos livres, vos cahiers, votre intelligence et votre volonté d’apprendre sont vos premières armes pour construire le Burkina Faso de demain », a-t-il conseillé. Il a également appelé les parents à assurer la continuité des enseignements reçus au camp, notamment en matière de discipline, de respect, de solidarité, de propreté et de sens du devoir. Au nom du parrain, le commandant de la 6e région militaire, le lieutenant-colonel Boubacar Badijan a salué l’initiative du Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, qu’il a qualifiée de « véritable creuset d’excellence civique et patriotique ». Il a également rendu hommage au parrain national du Camp Vacances Faso Mêbo, le général de brigade Ismaël Ousmane Diawari, Chef de l’Etat-major particulier du Président du Faso, pour son leadership et son accompagnement dans la mise en œuvre de l’initiative. S’adressant aux encadreurs, le commandant de la 6e région militaire a reconnu leur « travail titanesque », marqué par la patience, la rigueur et le don de soi. « Le camp vacances Faso Mêbo prend fin aujourd’hui, mais le véritable travail commence à la maison », a-t-il affirmé, invitant les parents à rester les premiers guides de leurs enfants sur le chemin de l’intégrité. Aux 525 campeurs, il a demandé de faire de la discipline le « fil conducteur » de leur vie et de porter partout les valeurs de paix, de civisme et de probité. Le Gouverneur de la région du Goulmou, Ram Joseph Kafando, a pour sa part salué l’ensemble des acteurs ayant contribué à la réussite de cette formation de dix jours. Il a remercié les acteurs militaires et civils, notamment aux encadreurs et à tous ceux qui ont œuvré à l’accompagnement et à la formation des 525 jeunes campeurs. Au nom des parents des campeurs, Yentéma Ouali a exprimé sa reconnaissance aux initiateurs et aux encadreurs pour cette formation offerte aux jeunes. Il a souhaité que le Camp Vacances Faso Mêbo se perpétue dans le temps et connaisse davantage d’ampleur lors des prochaines éditions. « C’est ainsi que nous pouvons avoir des citoyens nouveaux », a-t-il estimé, appelant à maintenir cette dynamique de formation et d’éducation citoyenne au profit de la jeunesse burkinabè. La promotion 2026 du Camp Vacances Faso Mèbo a été baptisée «Toyiro », un terme en langue bwaba qui signifie « L’avenir nous appartient ». Pour le commandant de la 6e région militaire, le lieutenant -colonel Boubacar Badijan, ce baptême traduit la responsabilité qui incombe à cette génération dans la construction du Burkina Faso. Les campeurs ont reçu des attestations de participation. Deux personnes physiques, distinguées par leur engagement dans la réussite de cette formation ont obtenu des attestations de reconnaissance. La cérémonie s’est achevée par une parade des 525 jeunes devant les autorités, leurs parents et les encadreurs, avant la déclaration officielle de clôture de l’édition 2026 du Camp Vacances Faso Mêbo au titre de la 6e région militaire. Agence d’information du Burkina KAC/HB/OO

items.title: Priscilla Ojo unveils son’s face on first birthday
items.description: Nigerian influencer Priscilla Ojo and her husband, Tanzanian singer Juma Jux, have unveiled their son Rakeem’s face as he marks his first birthday. The couple shared photographs of Prince Rakeem Mkambala on Instagram on Monday, after keeping his face private since his birth in Canada on Aug. 24, 2025. ”To our dearest son, watching you grow has been the biggest blessing. You are the most cheeky, happy, cleverest little pumpkin. You light up every room you walk into and we’re so proud to be your parents. ”365 days of loving you; cuddling you, and watching your beautiful personality shine. You are curious, so joyful, so smart and so full of life. You make every day better just by being you. ”We can’t believe how fast you’re growing, our little sunshine. May your life be filled with as much happiness as you have given us this past year. “We pray you grow up healthy, happy and full of purpose. We pray God guides your steps and orders your path. ”We pray you know how deeply you are loved, every single day. We pray your laughter never stops and your beautiful heart stays pure. ”You are our greatest answered prayer. Happy 1st Birthday our sunshine, we love you endlessly,” they wrote. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Rakeem was born in Canada on Aug. 24, 2025, to Priscilla and Jux, who had announced the pregnancy in July 2025. The couple had since shared photographs and videos of their son on social media, usually keeping his face private. Rakeem’s Instagram account, managed by his parents, also attracted more than 100,000 followers in spite of the absence of photographs showing his face. NAN reports that Priscilla and Jux held their wedding ceremonies in Nigeria and Tanzania in 2025 before welcoming their first child in Canada. items.title: UCC launches Africa Ocean Institute to strengthen coastal resilience
items.description: The University of Cape Coast (UCC) has officially launched the Africa Ocean Institute (AOI), a multidisciplinary platform aimed at advancing ocean knowledge, developing innovative solutions, and promoting the sustainable management of Africa’s coastal and marine resources. The launch, held at the Academic Board Chamber on the UCC campus, was presided over by the vice-chancellor, Professor Denis Worlanyo Aheto. The Registrar of the School, Gideon Abbeyquaye, Esq., said African coastal and marine ecosystems were facing several interconnected challenges. “African coastal and marine ecosystems are confronted by the combined challenges of climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution alongside illegal fishing, maritime insecurity, and the unsustainable exploitation of marine resources.” The launch marks the culmination of decades of work and vision in coastal management at UCC, dating back to the 1990s. In 1996, the university was identified as a forerunner of institutional advancement in integrated coastal management. This led to the establishment of a dedicated team to build awareness and capacity around coastal areas. Although the initial effort was later interrupted, the idea continued to develop and has now culminated in the establishment of the Africa Ocean Institute. Bringing together expertise Professor Denis Worlanyo Aheto said the idea for the institute had its roots in discussions held years ago. “The idea of this AOI, the discussion actually started in the corridors of Dakar…”he said. The AOI has been established as a multidisciplinary, science-based institutional platform that brings together the complementary expertise UCC has developed over the years. The institute has been designated as a graduate training hub and will operate alongside other prominent institutes within the university, including the Institute of Education Planning and Administration and the Institute for Development Studies. The strength of the AOI lies in bringing together three distinct but interconnected university entities. They are the Centre for Coastal Management , a World Bank Africa Centre of Excellence in Coastal Resilience; the Department of Fisheries and Aquaculture Science , which serves as an African Union Centre of Excellence for Training in Marine Fisheries and Coastal Zone Management; and the newly established Centre for Marine Affairs . The Centre for Coastal Management provides specialised knowledge in climate change, biological and coastal development and related areas. The Department of Fisheries and Aquaculture Science provides the academic foundation through its expertise in fisheries, aquatic sciences, aquaculture and related fields. The Centre for Marine Affairs contributes expertise in policy, governance, law and outreach, with a focus on the blue economy, ocean law, ocean governance and the relationship between marine resources, society and development. Together, the three entities are expected to provide a holistic approach to ocean studies. Focus on Africa’s blue economy The establishment of the institute is driven by the need to harness the opportunities presented by Africa’s oceans while addressing the challenges facing coastal and marine resources. Its mission is to “advance ocean knowledge, inspire solutions, and transform Africa’s Blue Future.” The blue economy represents a significant economic opportunity for the continent, with activities estimated to generate between US$296 billion and US$300 billion annually and support approximately 50 million jobs. Fisheries alone contribute an estimated 10 million tonnes of catch annually. If the catch were processed locally, it could potentially increase Africa’s gross domestic product by US$50 billion each year. The potential of the blue economy is particularly important given Africa’s geography. Of the continent’s 54 countries, 32 are coastal states, with many national capitals strategically located along the coast. The blue economy has consequently become an increasingly prominent part of Africa’s development agenda. Research and training The AOI is expected to provide an international platform for innovative, demand-driven and interdisciplinary research. It will also focus on training scientists, professionals, and practitioners to address the continent’s coastal and marine challenges. Ultimately, the institute is dedicated to promoting the sustainable management of physical coastal and marine resources. Through this approach, the Africa Ocean Institute seeks to help Africa harness the wealth of its oceans while preserving those resources for generations to come.

items.title: Blé tendre : la collecte en deçà des objectifs relance les importations
items.description: Après une suspension destinée à favoriser l’écoulement de la récolte nationale, les importations de blé tendre reprendront à partir de la mi-septembre. Le dispositif de soutien est réactivé jusqu’à la fin de l’année, alors que les volumes collectés restent inférieurs aux objectifs et que les stocks disponibles se contractent. Le Maroc réactivera, du 16 septembre au 31 décembre 2026, son mécanisme de soutien aux importations de blé tendre destiné à la minoterie. Le dispositif prévoit une prime forfaitaire destinée à compenser une partie du coût d’approvisionnement sur le marché international. Ses modalités ont été précisées dans une circulaire de l’Office national interprofessionnel des céréales et des légumineuses (ONICL), datée du 18 août. Cette reprise intervient après la suspension des importations décidée au début du mois de juin, qui visait à favoriser l’écoulement de la production nationale durant la période de commercialisation de la récolte. La campagne s’annonçait pourtant particulièrement favorable, avec une production céréalière attendue à près de 90 millions de quintaux sur quelque 3,9 millions d’hectares emblavés. La collecte du blé tendre est toutefois restée en deçà des objectifs. À fin juillet, environ 5 millions de quintaux avaient été collectés par les minotiers, alors que les professionnels évoquent désormais un volume proche de 6 millions de quintaux, pour un objectif initial de 15 millions. La période de collecte primable, initialement arrêtée au 31 juillet, avait d’ailleurs été prolongée jusqu’à fin août. Dans le même temps, les stocks constitués avant la suspension des importations se sont progressivement réduits. La reprise des achats à l’international vise ainsi à compléter les disponibilités nationales et à sécuriser l’approvisionnement des minoteries industrielles pour les prochains mois. Un mécanisme ajusté chaque mois La prime forfaitaire sera calculée sur la base de l’écart entre le prix de revient moyen du blé tendre importé à la sortie du port et un prix de référence fixé à 270 dirhams le quintal. Son montant sera révisé chaque mois afin de tenir compte de l’évolution des cours internationaux et des coûts d’acheminement. Le calcul prendra notamment en considération les importations en provenance de France, d’Allemagne, d’Argentine et des États-Unis. Lorsque l’écart entre les prix de revient de deux des origines les moins chères ne dépassera pas 30 dirhams par quintal, leur moyenne sera retenue. Au-delà de ce seuil, le calcul reposera sur le prix de revient de l’origine la moins chère, augmenté de 15 dirhams par quintal. Les cotations internationales du blé, le fret maritime à destination du Maroc et l’évolution de la parité entre le dollar et le dirham entreront également dans le calcul. Le dispositif prévoit par ailleurs des frais d’approche et une marge des importateurs fixée à 22,5 dirhams par quintal, maintenue constante pendant toute la période d’application. Le montant de la prime sera arrêté chaque mois par une commission réunissant des représentants des ministères de l’Économie et des Finances et de l’Agriculture ainsi que de l’ONICL. Celle-ci devra se réunir au plus tard le troisième jour ouvrable suivant la fin de chaque mois pour fixer le montant applicable au mois suivant. Un soutien directement lié aux livraisons aux minoteries Le bénéfice du mécanisme est conditionné à l’acheminement effectif du blé importé vers les minoteries industrielles. Les volumes concernés devront être livrés directement depuis les ports ou à partir des dépôts des organismes stockeurs, qui regroupent notamment les commerçants en céréales et légumineuses et les coopératives agricoles. Les quantités importées mais non livrées pourront entraîner la récupération des montants de la prime déjà versés. Les opérateurs devront également veiller à ce que les prix pratiqués répercutent le soutien accordé par les pouvoirs publics au niveau des prix à la consommation. Les mouvements du blé importé feront, de leur côté, l’objet d’un suivi à travers les déclarations adressées à l’ONICL. Le versement de la prime sera effectué en deux temps. Une première tranche représentant 80 % du montant sera accordée sur la base des quantités effectivement importées. Les 20 % restants seront versés après vérification des quantités réellement livrées aux minoteries industrielles et production des justificatifs requis. The post Blé tendre : la collecte en deçà des objectifs relance les importations appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Work begins to reclaim Lafa basin to reduce flooding in Mallam, Weija and surrounding areas
items.description: Work has begun to reclaim the Lafa water retention basin at Mallam as part of the government’s efforts to reduce the risk of flooding in Mallam, Weija, Dansoman and surrounding communities. The operation, being led by the 48 Engineer Regiment of the Ghana Armed Forces, is aimed at restoring the basin’s capacity after years of accumulated solid waste, siltation and illegal encroachment. The exercise involves dredging the basin, removing accumulated waste for disposal at a designated landfill site, demolishing illegal structures within the water reserve and constructing protective embankments to strengthen flood control measures. The operation is being coordinated by the Post-Flood Mitigation Task Force as part of a broader national effort to restore waterways and drainage channels across Accra following the devastating floods of June 29. The government has provided the resources and equipment required for the exercise, with similar flood mitigation works also underway at Oyarifa, East Legon and around the Kpeshie Lagoon. Authorities are urging residents and other members of the public to cooperate with the taskforce and refrain from activities that obstruct waterways or undermine efforts to manage flood risks. The reclamation of the Lafa basin is expected to improve its capacity to retain excess stormwater and help reduce the impact of flooding on communities downstream.

items.title: APC council: Kwankwaso faults Adedeji, Yakubu, as Melaye vows suit
items.description: The inclusion of the Chairman of the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS), Zacch Adedeji, and the Director-General of the Budget Office of the Federation, Taminu Yakubu, in the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council for the 2027 election has sparked criticism, with former Kogi West Senator Dino Melaye threatening legal action over Adedeji’s appointment. The APC had on Saturday unveiled its 108-member Presidential Campaign Council for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid, naming Tinubu as chairman, Vice President Kashim Shettima as Vice Chairman I and APC National Chairman, Nentawe Yilwatda, as Vice Chairman II. Former Zamfara State Governor Abdulaziz Yari was named Director-General of the council, while Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma was appointed Secretary. Ogun State Governor Dapo Abiodun was named Director of Fundraising, while Adedeji was appointed Deputy Director of Fundraising. Yakubu was named Treasurer. Reacting to the composition of the council, former Kogi West senator and chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Dino Melaye, said he would challenge Adedeji’s appointment in court, arguing that his role as head of the country’s revenue service could conflict with his campaign responsibilities. Melaye, who spoke in a video posted on his official X account on Sunday, questioned the decision to appoint a serving public official to a partisan campaign position. “And the most important aspect of the list that was released by the APC is to see the Chairman of FIRS—the body that collects our revenue as a nation—the Chairman of FIRS is the Deputy Director … for fundraising for Tinubu’s presidential campaign,” he said. Adedeji heads the Nigeria Revenue Service, formerly known as the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS). Melaye said the appointment raised questions about conflict of interest and compliance with the Public Service Rules and public service ethics. “As a lawyer, by the grace of God, on Monday, I’m going to court. We have to test that,” he said. He added that Adedeji, as a serving public official, was expected to comply with the rules governing public service conduct. “If that is not conflict of interest, I don’t know what else it would be,” Melaye said, adding that he would continue to oppose Tinubu’s re-election bid. Melaye also criticised the decision to make Tinubu chairman of his own campaign council, describing the arrangement as unprecedented and “disgraceful.” He questioned why the presidential candidate would also head the campaign council and alleged that the arrangement suggested a lack of confidence within the ruling party. The former senator also described the 108-member council as “very, very, very bogus.” Meanwhile, Musa Rabiu Kwankwaso, vice-presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), also faulted the inclusion of Adedeji and Yakubu in the campaign council. Kwankwaso said the appointments undermined the institutional neutrality of the agencies headed by the two officials, particularly given their responsibilities for public revenue and national finances. “The leadership of critical public institutions demands neutrality, integrity and public confidence. It is therefore legitimate to ask whether the responsibilities of senior officials entrusted with managing public revenue and national finances can appropriately coexist with senior partisan campaign roles,” he said in a statement on Sunday. He said the composition of the campaign council should concern Nigerians, particularly amid economic hardship, unemployment, insecurity and pressure on essential public services. Kwankwaso also appealed to Yari to reconsider his acceptance of the Director-General position, arguing that the former Zamfara governor understood the security and economic challenges facing the North-West and the country. “I therefore will be surprised if, in his good conscience, he will lead a campaign whose principal objective is to secure the continuation of a government under which many of the people he once governed, and other innocent Nigerians, remain trapped in these challenges,” he said. Kwankwaso described the 2027 election as a contest between Nigerians facing hardship and those he accused of benefiting from the existing system. He urged Nigerians to reject what he described as “continued oppression” and demand accountable and people-oriented governance. The post APC council: Kwankwaso faults Adedeji, Yakubu, as Melaye vows suit appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: We supported Ogogo’s treatment, did everything to save him – Yayi
items.description: Ogun State All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate, Solomon Adeola, has expressed grief over the death of veteran actor Taiwo Hassan, popularly known as Ogogo, recalling his efforts to support the actor’s medical treatment before his death. Ogogo died on Sunday, August 23, 2026, aged 66. The movie star battled stage-four cancer. Adeola, also known as Yayi, said he and his wife, Temitope, stood by Ogogo and his family throughout his illness and made efforts to ensure he received appropriate medical attention. In a tribute signed by the couple and shared on Facebook on Monday, Adeola said Ogogo’s death was painful, particularly after the actor’s “courageous battle” with illness and the widespread hopes and prayers for his recovery. He said the family remained optimistic that the actor would survive the health challenge and return to his loved ones and admirers. “During those difficult moments, we stood closely with him and his family, supporting his treatment and doing everything humanly possible to ensure that he received the necessary medical care. “We remained hopeful and prayerful that he would overcome the illness and return to the family, friends and countless admirers who cherished him. Sadly, despite all efforts, it has pleased Almighty God to call him home. Indeed, God knows best,” the statement read. Adeola described the late actor as a man whose significance went beyond his achievements in the entertainment industry, calling him a “dear brother” and a distinguished son of Ilaro and Ogun West. He noted that Ogogo’s decades-long career had entertained generations while making a significant contribution to the development of Nigeria’s film industry. “Alhaji Taiwo Hassan was more than an accomplished veteran of the entertainment industry to us; he was a dear brother and a proud son of Ilaro and Ogun West, whose remarkable career brought joy to generations and contributed immensely to the growth and development of the Nigerian film industry. “His talent, humility and enduring body of work will ensure that his memory lives on,” Adeola said. The senator condoled with Ogogo’s wife, children and other family members, as well as the people of Ilaro and Yewaland and the actor’s colleagues and associates in the entertainment industry. Ogogo’s daughters, Kaira and Lima Taiwo, had previously acknowledged Adeola’s assistance to their father during his illness. The post We supported Ogogo’s treatment, did everything to save him – Yayi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: No minimum salary required for Republic Bank mortgage – Head of Mortgage Banking
items.description: The Head of Mortgage Banking at Republic Bank, Dan Adjetey Morhenu, has assured prospective homeowners that the bank does not have a minimum salary requirement for customers seeking mortgage financing. According to him, Republic Bank’s mortgage solutions are designed to accommodate customers across different income levels, with the financing arrangement depending largely on an applicant’s income and the type of property they intend to acquire. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Monday, August 24, Mr Morhenu said the bank could support customers at different stages of their homeownership journey, including those who may need to acquire land before gradually developing their properties. His comments followed the conclusion of the 2026 JoyNews-Republic Bank Habitat Fair at the Achimota Retail Centre, where prospective homeowners engaged financial institutions, property developers and other players in the housing sector. The three-day mini-fair, held from Friday, August 21 to Sunday, August 23, provided patrons with an opportunity to seek information on mortgages, property acquisition, construction financing and other housing solutions. ‘We don’t have a minimum salary’ Mr Morhenu said one of the most frequently asked questions at the fair was the minimum salary required to qualify for a mortgage. He explained that Republic Bank does not impose a fixed salary threshold, stressing that people with different income levels could explore mortgage options. “One of the key questions that came up was what is the minimum salary to qualify for a mortgage, and we kept hammering that we don’t have a minimum salary. No matter the amount you earn as income, there is a mortgage for you,” he said. He explained, however, that an applicant’s income would determine the type of mortgage arrangement and homeownership path that would be most suitable. Customers with lower incomes, he said, could begin by acquiring land and gradually progress to construction, while those with higher incomes could potentially purchase completed properties. “Based on the quantum of income, some people may have to start from the land and we walk them through the building. Some also, because they earn so much, are able to acquire properties immediately,” he explained. Mr Morhenu said Republic Bank’s approach was not simply to provide loans but to structure mortgage solutions around customers’ individual financial circumstances. He also highlighted the bank’s fixed mortgage rates, saying they provide borrowers with greater certainty and help them manage their finances throughout the repayment period. “At Republic Bank, our rates are fixed. We fix it because we want you to manage your cash flow, so it is not just about purchasing a house; we are also managing your cash flow for you,” he said. ‘There was a long queue before we set up’ Mr Morhenu also described the turnout at the Habitat Fair as unexpectedly high, saying a queue had already formed at the Achimota Retail Centre before exhibitors had completed setting up on the opening day. “It was exciting. I was quite surprised that even before we set up on Friday, there was a long queue at the mall waiting to have a conversation with not just Republic Bank, but the other exhibitors,” he said. He said the strong interest continued throughout the three-day event, with Republic Bank’s booth remaining busy until late on Friday. According to him, the bank’s mortgage team stayed until about 8:30pm on the opening day to attend to the last customer. The interest continued on Saturday, when more members of the public visited the fair and sought information on mortgage financing. “We had our fellow bankers who came around to ask questions, we had government workers, expatriates who came around and we had to take our time because mortgages are not just a one-time decision that you take,” he said. Mr Morhenu stressed that purchasing a home was a major financial commitment and required careful discussions between prospective borrowers and mortgage specialists. He said the bank was prepared to spend sufficient time with customers to understand their financial circumstances and guide them towards suitable mortgage options. Republic Bank offers refinancing for dollar mortgages The Republic Bank executive also addressed challenges faced by some borrowers who had taken US dollar-denominated mortgages from other financial institutions. He disclosed that the bank undertook several refinancing arrangements in 2022 for customers who were servicing dollar loans but were struggling with the financial burden. “In 2022, we had to refinance a lot of these loans. They had US dollar loans with other banks. They approached us to refinance them in cedis, so most of them are okay now,” he said. He urged customers who may still be struggling with foreign currency-denominated mortgage obligations not to abandon their properties but to approach Republic Bank to explore possible refinancing options. “If there are some of them who are still struggling, don’t walk away from your property. They should come and speak to us so that we can refinance them into cedis,” Mr Morhenu said. He assured such customers that the bank could consider flexible repayment arrangements depending on their circumstances. ‘We were really overwhelmed with the numbers’ Also speaking about the Habitat Fair, Mortgage Specialist at Republic Bank (Ghana) PLC, Elizabeth Abena Anokware Amedeka, expressed appreciation to members of the public for their strong participation. She said the turnout reflected growing interest among Ghanaians in understanding how mortgages work and the steps involved in securing a home. “We want to thank the public for the massive turnout. It was great; people asked the right questions about mortgages and how to start. We were really overwhelmed with the numbers,” she said. Ms Amedeka encouraged members of the public to participate in future editions of the fair, assuring them that Republic Bank was ready to guide prospective homeowners throughout the homeownership process. She said the bank’s support went beyond providing financing, with mortgage specialists available to guide customers from the initial stages through to acquiring their homes. “Republic Bank is ready to walk you through this journey and we are ready to assist you from the beginning of the process to you picking up your keys,” she said.

items.title: What a Bicentennial Baby Knows
items.description: Thirteen seconds after midnight on July 4, 1976, Karen Steele was born in Montclair, New Jersey, and was anointed the first “bicentennial baby.” Newspaper articles followed. President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty, sent a note to the family. And then it kind of became a thing. Any baby born that year was treated like they had emerged playing the fife and drums. In Mobile, Alabama, new mothers received a commemorative blanket. In Covington, Louisiana, a hospital handed out (for $2.50) special “bicentennial baby” certificates on faux parchment, a “memento that can be framed and cherished as a family heirloom for endless generations.” This was a year of jaw-dropping kitsch , an explosion of red, white, and blue everything —toilet paper, lollipops, even condoms (pleading: One Time for Old Glory ). Branding newborns this way became part of the general patriotic fun. And although the tchotchkes surely ended up moldering in a red, white, and blue landfill somewhere, the label stuck. I know: I was one of those babies, born in August 1976. Being a bicentennial baby was not anything I ever thought about all that much. In fact, it was really only when meeting another person born in 1976 that it came up at all. Oh, you’re a bicentennial baby too , one of us would say to the other, smiling dumbly. This was a secret handshake that opened zero doors. But unlike other indelible parts of my identity that felt small in their particularity—like being the child of immigrants or being nearsighted—having my birth hitched somehow to the history of the country, to its forward motion, felt big whenever I was reminded of it. Beyond the horror of realizing that five of my current lifespans stacked up is all that separates me now from Benjamin Franklin, I’ve been thinking about this cohort of which I’m a part. Expounding on the significance of one’s own generation can lead rapidly to wild generalization, self-absorption, and some misplaced nostalgia. I know this. But I’m convinced that my fellow bicentennial babies and I have been through something unique. We’ve followed a distinct arc over the past 50 years: one of disillusionment. Better than most, we understand the disjunctions of our present because they happened at crucial inflection points alongside the timeline of our lives. We were born during a period of palate-cleansing. The Vietnam War was over. President Richard Nixon had, in 1974, resigned after Watergate, a redemptive scandal that renewed people’s faith in self-government. Journalists—yes, journalists —were sex symbols. Robert Redford played Bob Woodward in All the President’s Men . And the peanut farmer Jimmy Carter, a man who campaigned teeth-first, would be elected president in the fall, having promised a new era of idealism. [ Read: Inside America’s ugly birthday battle ] I don’t remember any of this, of course, but babies like me were launched into an atmosphere of reawakened good vibes. When Time magazine commissioned the polling firm Yankelovich, Skelly & White to gauge the country’s temperature from June to September of 1976, the company found a 10 percent jump in positivity on its “state of the nation index” between those months, the most rapid increase it had seen since it began tracking the metric. The following years were also a time of crime and stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis, but at least by the indicators used by pollsters to determine collective mood, things continued to get generally sunnier into the ’80s. “The Zeitgeist has turned zesty,” Kurt Andersen wrote in a 1984 assessment of that year’s numbers. “The U.S. is at peace, and between rising employment and fading inflation, the economy is aglow. Americans are feeling more sanguine and comfortable about their country than they have felt in two decades. A rebirth of the American spirit, as Carter dearly hoped five summers ago? It sure feels like it.” I remember this optimism and confidence. On November 9, 1989, I sat watching television with my grandfather—a Holocaust survivor who that day, and most days, had his shirt off and a captain’s hat on his head. The Berlin Wall was coming down. This happened when we bicentennial babies were 13 and highly impressionable. Look at them , my grandfather said, his voice breaking, as people pick-axed their way out of East Germany. I recall the total elation on their faces when they finally broke through, and then the bracing thought that they were trying to get to the side where I already lived. The author in 1978 with his parents, sitting on his grandfather's Cadillac (Courtesy of Gal Beckerman) For many young Americans in those years, a feeling of transcendence was possible. You had a sense that good fortune had placed you somewhere that everyone in the world wished they could be. At the same time, that wider world, with its crumbling empires and ethnic cleansing and genocides, seemed very far away. Even the Gulf War of the early ’90s appeared, to those of us safe at home, as a ghostly green video game playing on CNN, transmitted from somewhere hard to recognize as real. You may not believe me when I tell you that I read Francis Fukuyama’s The End of History and the Last Man at 19, for fun, when I was a junior and living abroad in France . But I did, and then after college I went into the Peace Corps and lived in a village in Cameroon for two years. Although many of the people there thought that I was working for the CIA (I was not), I felt I was doing something uncomplicatedly wholesome, even a little patriotic. We were 25 when 9/11 happened. I moved to New York City in October of that year, like a salmon swimming upstream—or like a salmon following a girl. Everywhere were posters of missing people. During my first days of couch surfing, New Yorkers were further terrorized by anthrax spores sent through the mail, addressed to political and media targets. That terrible fall was a hinge moment for all Americans but maybe especially for us young adults, who were also at a hinge moment in our lives, suddenly vulnerable and less innocent in new ways, feeling silly for having believed that history could have an end. [ Jerusalem Demsas: The end of Francis Fukuyama ] I haven’t mentioned the internet yet, but it also came around for us as adulthood hit. I got my first email address in college and accessed my inbox in the library basement at a computer lab that perpetually smelled like Doritos. It was all so new that you could forget to send a paper to a professor and then offer the excuse that the email probably just got lost . I spent a lot of time outside that library, chatting, with nothing in my hands besides a cigarette. I think I knew someone who had a beeper. We got flip phones in our 20s. We were in our early 30s when the first iPhone arrived and Facebook showed up. We were told that these were revolutionary tools. Maybe we believed this more than other people did, still being relatively young and feeling like we were being handed powerful megaphones in our prime—a chance to make change, to connect. Then the tools congealed into yet more products that would waste our hours and make us feel terrible about ourselves and our fellow citizens. We made lives against the backdrop of distant wars, unceasing notifications popping up on our phones. The year we turned 40, Donald Trump was elected president. Four years later came COVID. Just as we were balancing more and more—perhaps children, a challenging job, ailing parents—the world seemed to conspire to keep our heads spinning. In these past few years, before we and the country hit our big milestones, we were assaulted by panicked warnings about the state of American democracy—and the future of the entire human race. What has AI been up to over the past few days? Creating new viruses and independently cyberhacking, it appears. We are less naive, though more exhausted. It has not been lost on us that the people warning that AI could lead to our extinction are the same people who invented it. This is a pattern we’re familiar with now: Technology gives us something with one hand while robbing us of something else with the other. I’m leaving out a lot. We also had private joys and tragedies totally impervious to what America writ large was up to. But I can distinguish a progression toward an increased sense of emergency, toward alienation, toward a mournfulness that makes me read the newspaper through my fingers most days. I don’t think this is the birthday blues talking—or, if I’m honest, maybe not just the birthday blues. It’s also the metrics: about loneliness and economic stagnation and political polarization and the whole insane technological surround sound of our lives. My point is that bicentennial babies, regardless of their individual circumstances, have all been strapped into the first row of this ride. Someone born on America’s centennial, in 1876, could well have argued that they had witnessed much more consequential change by their 50th birthday. They might have gushed about the expansion of railroads and telegraphs, about seeing the first airplanes, telephones, and radios, and then explained what it was like to face the reality that as many as 20 million people could be killed in a single war. I wouldn’t want to go head-to-head with them. Every generation has its story. But we bicentennial babies have lived through a major rupture. For all else that might be good in our lives—and I’m lucky to have a lot that’s good—this is not such an exuberant place to find ourselves at 50. [ Read: Trump’s 250th celebration is a fiasco ] Can we imagine anyone proudly calling the babies born this year—what? semiquincentennial sprouts ? A mouthful, granted. But that’s not what makes it sound strange. Behind the “bicentennial babies” moniker was a kind of hope. We would be the Americans of the future. And we would be moving toward that future not with dread but with anticipation. Whatever one’s political affiliation, people do not have much enthusiasm these days when they picture where we’re headed. When the Pew Research Center surveyed Americans just before this year’s semiquincentennial, 59 percent of respondents said that the country’s best years were behind it. Asked to imagine the United States 50 years from now, 44 percent were pessimistic and only 28 percent were optimistic. Perhaps most telling, 27 percent chose neither option; they just felt blah . Recently, Conan O’Brian, speaking on the podcast The Rest Is History , talked about the “undiluted joy” he remembers feeling as a preteen experiencing the bicentennial. Now: “It’s very hard for some people, maybe, to just say, I’m really excited about our 250th when our current state is so divided .” I can’t conceive of myself being around for the tricentennial—and if I did suggest living to 100, my mother might faint from all the spitting she’d have to do to ward off the evil eye. But if I do make it there, I will have lived through a third of the country’s existence. I’ll have a lot more data to work with. Will 2026 appear in retrospect as another hinge, or simply as a snapshot of us—mouths open and eyes closed, as in an amusement-park photograph—mid–free fall? Will there be self-correction or a piling-on of bad decisions? Disintegration or newfound connection? No one can really tell. Though I do know what I would like on my 50th birthday and the country’s 250th: something for us to look forward to. ​​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .

items.title: ‘It was exciting’ – Republic Bank executive recounts huge turnout at Habitat Fair
items.description: Head of Mortgage Banking at Republic Bank, Dan Adjetey Morhenu, has described the strong public turnout at the 2026 JoyNews-Republic Bank Habitat Fair as “exciting”, saying interest in the event was evident even before exhibitors had opened their stands. According to him, a long queue had already formed at the Achimota Retail Centre on Friday, August 21, with patrons eager to engage Republic Bank and other exhibitors on homeownership, mortgage financing and housing solutions. “It was exciting. I was quite surprised that even before we set up on Friday, there was a long queue at the mall waiting to have a conversation with not just Republic Bank, but the other exhibitors,” Mr Morhenu said. He was speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Monday, August 24, while reflecting on the three-day Habitat Fair, which ended at the Achimota Retail Centre on Sunday, August 23. The event brought together prospective homeowners and players in Ghana’s housing and construction sector, giving patrons the opportunity to explore options for building, buying, financing or improving their homes. Mr Morhenu said the level of interest was so high that Republic Bank’s mortgage team had to extend its operations beyond the scheduled closing time on the opening day. “On Friday, we didn’t close early. We had to wait for the last person to leave our booth before we closed. That was around 8:30pm,” he said. ‘Mortgages are not just a one-time decision’ The strong turnout continued into Saturday, with more patrons visiting the fair to engage exhibitors and seek information on mortgage financing. Mr Morhenu said the bank interacted with people from diverse backgrounds, including fellow bankers, government workers and expatriates. “Then it followed through on Saturday. As for Saturday, people are home and so a lot of people came around. We had our fellow bankers who came around to ask, we had government workers, expatriates who came around and we had to take our time,” he said. He said the bank could not rush its engagements with prospective customers because taking a mortgage was a significant long-term financial commitment. “Mortgages are not just a one-time decision that you take, so we had to take our time for everybody and then we closed off on Sunday,” he added. One of the most frequently asked questions during the fair, he said, was the minimum salary required to qualify for a mortgage. Mr Morhenu explained that Republic Bank does not have a fixed minimum salary threshold, allowing people with different income levels to explore mortgage options. “One of the key questions that came up was what is the minimum salary to qualify for a mortgage, and we kept hammering that we don’t have a minimum salary. No matter the amount you earn as income, there is a mortgage for you,” he said. He explained, however, that a customer’s income would determine the type of mortgage arrangement and homeownership option that would be most suitable. Customers with lower incomes, he said, could begin their homeownership journey by acquiring land and gradually progressing to construction, while those with higher incomes could potentially purchase completed properties. “It’s just that based on the quantum of income, some people may have to start from the land and we walk them through the building. Some also, because they earn so much, are able to acquire properties immediately,” he explained. Republic Bank highlights fixed mortgage rates Mr Morhenu also highlighted Republic Bank’s fixed mortgage rates, saying the arrangement gives customers greater certainty in managing their finances throughout the repayment period. He said the bank’s mortgage offering went beyond simply financing the purchase of a property to helping customers manage their cash flow. “At Republic Bank, our rates are fixed. We fix it because we want you to manage your cash flow. So it is not just about purchasing a house; we are also managing your cash flow for you,” he said. According to him, the approach enables prospective homeowners to better understand their financial obligations and plan their finances around their mortgage repayments. Mr Morhenu also spoke about challenges faced by some customers who had taken US dollar-denominated mortgage loans from other banks. He disclosed that Republic Bank, in 2022, assisted some of these customers by refinancing their dollar-denominated loans into cedi facilities. “In 2022, we had to refinance a lot of these loans. They had US dollar loans with other banks. They approached us to refinance them in cedis, so most of them are okay now,” he said. READ ALSO: JoyNews-Republic Bank Habitat Fair finale turns homeownership dreams into real possibilities He urged customers who were still struggling with such loans not to abandon their properties but to approach Republic Bank to explore possible refinancing arrangements. “If there are some of them who are still struggling, don’t walk away from your property. They should come and speak to us so that we can refinance them into cedis,” Mr Morhenu said. He added that the bank would be willing to consider flexible terms for eligible customers to help them manage their mortgage obligations. ‘We were really overwhelmed with numbers’ Mortgage Specialist at Republic Bank (Ghana) PLC, Elizabeth Abena Anokware Amedeka, also expressed gratitude to the public for the strong turnout at the Habitat Fair. She said the event provided an important opportunity for prospective homeowners to ask practical questions and gain a better understanding of how to begin their homeownership journey. “We want to thank the public for the massive turnout. It was great. People asked the right questions about mortgage and how to start. We were really overwhelmed with numbers,” she said. Ms Amedeka encouraged members of the public to participate in subsequent editions of the fair, assuring them that Republic Bank was prepared to support customers throughout the mortgage process. “We want to say don’t miss the next session because Republic Bank is ready to walk you through this journey and we are ready to assist you from the beginning of the process to you picking up your keys,” she said. She stressed that the bank’s role went beyond providing loans, saying it was committed to guiding customers through the various stages of securing a home.

items.title: Newly elected members of AJK Legislative Assembly take oath of office
items.description: MUZAFFARABAD: Newly elected members of the AJK Legislative Assembly were administered the oath of office by outgoing Speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar on Monday. Assembly Secretary Amjed Latif Abbasi read out the notifications of the 38 members elected from the territorial and refugee constituencies in the phased elections, as well as those of the eight members elected by them on reserved seats. Shortly after the announcement of the results, all newly elected members took the oath at the hands of the outgoing speaker, who failed to retain his seat in the elections. The members then signed the oath register in the order of their constituencies. PML-N’s Ahmed Raza Qadri moved a motion seeking the suspension of the rules that prescribed a bar on certain times for elections to the offices of speaker, deputy speaker and leader of the house. On a point of order, PPP’s Abdul Majid Khan noted that although the PML-N had a majority and could suspend the rules, it should avoid holding the session on the 12th of Rabi-ul-Awwal — Eid-i-Miladun Nabi, widely commemorated as the birthday of Prophet Muhammad (Peace Be Upon Him) — out of respect for the sanctity of the day. The chair, however, said there was no harm in holding the session and conducting the election process on that day. “The transition of power should take place as early as possible, and it is good that on 12 Rabi-ul-Awwal, members will pay tributes to the Holy Prophet (Peace Be Upon Him) from the floor of the house,” he said, amid desk-thumping by PML-N legislators. PML-N wins 5, PPP wins 2 reserved seats The PML-N bagged five while the PPP won two of the seven reserved seats that were up for grabs in the Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Legislative Assembly on Monday. Under Article 22(1) of the AJK Constitution, the Legislative Assembly consists of 53 members, including 45 members elected directly through adult franchise and eight members chosen by directly elected representatives. The reserved seats include five seats for women and one each for Ulema-i-Din or Mashaikh well-versed in the teachings of Islam, Jammu and Kashmir State subjects residing abroad, and technocrats and other professionals. PML-N’s Chaudhry Abdul Rehman Arain was the only candidate to have submitted his nomination papers for the seat reserved for state subjects residing abroad. He was consequently declared elected unopposed. After polling for the remaining seats on Monday, PML-N’s Sehrish Qamar, Maryam Idrees and Maryam Zaman, also known as Maryam Kashmiri, secured one seat each reserved for women. Seven votes were polled for each of them, as were for PPP’s Farzana Yaqoob, who claimed the fourth reserved seat for women. There were just two more contenders — PML-N’s Riffat Abid and PPP’s Zobia Khurshid Raja — vying for the seats for women whose votes were tied at five. Eventually, Raja was declared the winner for the last seat left, with the result being decided by drawing lots. For the seat reserved for Ulema and Mashaikh, PML-N’s Mohammad Mazhar Saeed won against his sole contender, PPP’s Hafiz Tariq Mahmood, after garnering 26 votes — almost double than Mahmood’s 12. Similarly, PML-N’s Barrister Syed Iftikhar Gillani also bagged 26 votes to claim the seat reserved for technocrats and professionals, beating PPP’s Sahibzada Zulfiqar Ali by 14 votes. Shortly after their election, the Election Commission notified the successful candidates. In days preceding Monday’s polls, elections to seven of the 45 directly elected seats — five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district — could not be held due to the law and order situation in the region. As a result, the 38 members elected so far, representing 84.4 per cent of the directly elected membership, participated in the reserved seat elections. AJK polls The elections in the region, originally scheduled for July 27, were divided into phases over security concerns amid unrest in the region. The first phase was held on July 27, the second on Aug 2 and the third on Aug 10. The third phase was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division, which comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli because of concerns over the law and order situation. So far, in the direct elections to 38 constituencies, the PML-N has secured 25 seats while the PPP won 12. The lone MLA-elect of the Awami Dast-o-Bazu party has also joined hands with the PML-N . The PPP has alleged widespread rigging in the polls, with the party also ramping up its criticism of the ruling PML-N in recent days. Last week, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said that a genuine alliance with the PML-N was not possible until their grievances regarding the AJK polls were addressed as he established formal contact with the PTI and offered to cooperate with the party in Parliament. Speaking to the media, the PPP chairman alleged that the AJK election process had been made controversial for political interests. He alleged that the federal government’s political and administrative machinery had remained active in AJK throughout the six-phase election process, raising serious questions over its transparency. The PPP, he said, had raised its objections before the Election Commission, parliament and other constitutional forums, but the PML-N had failed to address its concerns or engage in meaningful dialogue after the polls. Moreover, he said the commitments and political understandings reached with the PML-N before the prime minister’s election had not been honoured. The PPP had cooperated in the wider national interest, he said, but there could be no genuine alliance with the PML-N unless the party’s concerns over the AJK elections were addressed and political commitments fulfilled. He pointed out that the government needed PPP’s votes for several important laws, constitutional amendments and difficult bills. He said legislation could not be forced through on the basis of a majority or through coercion. The discord between the PPP and PML-N was also apparent in the National Assembly on Aug 18, when the former managed to compel the government to virtually suspend the heavy legislative agenda for the day, which included 21 bills. On Aug 20, when the lower house of Parliament passed two bills pertaining to the military and nuclear command structure, the PPP also objected to the manner in which the legislation was presented. While the party ultimately voted in favour of the bills, Bilawal lashed out at the government for not taking ruling allies on board.

items.title: GoldBod losses remain key on Minority agenda as Parliament reconvenes – Afenyo-Markin
items.description: Minority Leader in Parliament, Alexander Afenyo-Markin, has reaffirmed the New Patriotic Party (NPP) Caucus’ commitment to investigating the reported loss of more than US$1.7 billion linked to the Bank of Ghana’s Domestic Gold Purchase Programme and the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod). Mr Afenyo-Markin made the statement after meeting NPP flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia at his private residence in Accra on Monday morning. According to the Minority Leader, the meeting focused on party matters and key issues confronting the Minority ahead of Parliament’s emergency sitting. He said Dr Bawumia commended the Minority Caucus for its work and encouraged members to continue holding the government accountable. “He commended the Minority for its efforts so far.” Mr Afenyo-Markin said the reported loss, which he described as equivalent to about 1.5% of Ghana’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP), would remain a key issue for the Minority as Parliament reconvenes. “I further informed him that this colossal loss, under the watch of GoldBod and the Bank of Ghana, is firmly on the Minority’s agenda as Parliament reconvenes today.” He said the Minority would pursue the matter in the interest of the Ghanaian public and seek answers over the circumstances surrounding the reported loss. “We remain resolute in this commitment, and we will not relent until the Ghanaian people receive the answers they deserve.” The Minority has been pushing for parliamentary scrutiny of the reported losses associated with the Domestic Gold Purchase Programme, with the NPP Caucus expected to pursue its motion for an inquiry when the House resumes.

items.title: Russia’s second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes
items.description: Warehouses belonging to Russia’s second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes. Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes. Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country’s biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened “Pandora’s box” by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv’s “most sensitive economic sectors”. Russia has targeted Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians. Ozon said “a fire broke out” at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday. The company said earlier that a “major fire” was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site. Russia’s defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia’s children’s rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital. Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated. Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan. Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%. When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was “working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation”. The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon’s site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured. Following that strike, Ukraine’s defence ministry said on Saturday: “Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy’s logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole. “After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon’s turn.” Meanwhile, in Ukraine’s Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region’s head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram. Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia’s first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country. Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points. The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians. Both companies have been described as “Russia’s Amazon” and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia’s economically active population. In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances. But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments. This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses. The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies.

items.title: Nearly three million Teslas recalled in China over hidden door handles
items.description: Minimalistic door handles became a signature feature of electric vehicles (EVs), but the controversial designs are now at the centre of China’s biggest car recall, affecting more than 4 million vehicles. The recall, which includes 2.98 million Chinese-made Teslas, follows safety concerns that the hidden door handles are difficult to locate and open in emergency situations. Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely. The recalled vehicles will have a warning label stuck on the interior door and receive a software update to automatically lower the windows in a crash. The designs have come under scrutiny after two fatal crashes in China involving Xiaomi EVs, in which power failures were suspected to have prevented doors from being opened. Tesla said in a statement on Friday that it was recalling some of its Model 3, Y, S and X vehicles due to door handles that are “difficult to identify and operate because their colour is similar to the interior trim”. “In extreme situations such as a severe collision causing the vehicle’s low-voltage system to fail, this could hinder occupants from quickly opening the doors to escape and impede rescue efforts by those outside the vehicle, posing a safety hazard,” it said. Tesla said it would place warning labels on the recalled vehicles and issue a software update to automatically lower a vehicle’s windows after a collision. It is not clear if the affected firms plan to make a similar recall for the rest of the world. The BBC has contacted Tesla, XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely for comment. The use of hidden handle designs has “snowballed” after Chinese brands were quick to copy the “sleek” look of Tesla’s Model S sedan since 2014, said Tu Le, the founder of consultancy Sino Auto Insights. The use of warning labels and a software update is more of a “band-aid” than a lasting solution for the issue, he added. In February, Chinese authorities announced a ban on hidden door handles. Under new rules due to take effect on 1 January 2027, cars will only be allowed to be sold in China if they have a mechanical release on both the inside and outside of their doors. Tesla’s door handles were also involved in a probe by US safety regulators after reports that they suddenly stopped working, leaving children trapped in the cars. In July, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggested creating a new formal safety standard for all carmakers. The BBC has contacted the agency for comment.

items.title: Eid-el-Maulud: Akpabio felicitates Muslims, seeks prayers for peace, unity
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — President of the Senate, Senator Godswill Akpabio, has felicitated the Muslim Ummah in Nigeria and across the world on the occasion of Eid-el-Maulud, commemorating the birth of Prophet Muhammad (SAW). In a congratulatory message signed by his Special Adviser on Media and Publicity, Hon. Eseme Eyiboh, Akpabio described the life and teachings of the Holy Prophet as a timeless example of compassion, tolerance, humility and service to humanity. “As we commemorate this sacred day, I urge our Muslim brothers and sisters to reflect on the virtues of the Prophet and to offer special prayers for peace, unity and progress in our dear country, Nigeria,” he said. The Senate President noted that Nigeria’s strength lies in its diversity and called on citizens to embrace love, forgiveness and mutual respect, regardless of their faith or ethnicity. He said, “In these times, our nation needs the prayers of all religious leaders and faithful. Let us use this period to pray for our leaders, for security, economic prosperity and for the unity that binds us together as one people under God.” Akpabio reaffirmed the commitment of the 10th Senate under his leadership to promoting legislation and policies that protect religious freedom, foster national cohesion and improve the welfare of all Nigerians. He also felicitated President Bola Tinubu and Vice President Kashim Shettima, wishing the Muslim community a peaceful and joyous Eid-el-Maulud celebration.
